laws.title: Mobile Phone Use While Driving — Prohibited
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — Handheld use banned; hands-free permitted
laws.fullDescription: South Australia prohibits use of handheld mobile phones while driving. South Australia has increased mobile phone penalties. Phone detection cameras being introduced. Hands-free operation via Bluetooth or dashboard mount is permitted.
laws.penalty: $534 fine + 3 demerit points.
exceptions: Hands-free (mounted or Bluetooth)
Emergency calls to 000
Emergency services on duty

quiz.q: What is the fine for using a handheld mobile phone while driving in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: In South Australia, using a handheld mobile phone while driving attracts a fine of $534 and 3 demerit points.

laws.title: Recreational Fishing Licence — Recreational Fishing Licence required
laws.subtitle: Fisheries Management Act 2007 (SA) — Recreational Fishing Licence (RFL) required
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: South Australia requires a Recreational Fishing Licence (RFL) for most recreational fishing. Licences are available online and at tackle shops. Bag and size limits apply. Bag and size limits apply to most species. Commercial fishing requires separate licensing.
laws.penalty: Fishing without a licence: infringement notice $315–$5,000.
exceptions: Children under certain ages may be exempt
Fishing in exempted waters
Indigenous peoples exercising traditional fishing rights

quiz.q: Is a recreational fishing licence required in South Australia?
options: No — fishing is free in SA
Yes — a Recreational Fishing Licence is required for most fishing
quiz.explanation: South Australia requires a Recreational Fishing Licence for most fishing activities.

laws.title: Drink Driving — 0.05 BAC Limit
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — BAC ≥ 0.05 is illegal for most drivers
laws.fullDescription: Australia harmonised its drink-driving limit at 0.05% BAC in 1992. South Australia enforces this through Random Breath Testing (RBT). Zero BAC applies to learner and P-plate (provisional) drivers and heavy vehicle operators. South Australia uses Random Breath Testing and roadside drug testing. SA has a strong road safety enforcement history.
laws.penalty: Low-range (0.05–0.079): $511 fine + 3-month suspension (first). High-range (0.15+): $511–$1,300 + 6-month suspension + possible imprisonment.
exceptions: Full licence holders: 0.05% limit
Learner/P-plate drivers: 0.00% (zero BAC)
Commercial/bus/truck drivers: 0.00%

quiz.q: What is the general blood alcohol limit for fully licensed drivers in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Australia's drink-driving limit for fully licensed drivers is 0.05% BAC — lower than the US/Canada 0.08%. Learner and provisional drivers must have 0.00%.

laws.title: Open Alcohol in Vehicles
laws.subtitle: Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW) — No open liquor in vehicle
laws.fullDescription: South Australia prohibits consuming alcohol in a motor vehicle and carrying open alcohol containers accessible to the driver or passengers while driving. NSW prohibits a person from driving or being in charge of a vehicle while consuming alcohol.
laws.penalty: Fine up to $2,200.
exceptions: Sealed containers may be transported in the boot
Passengers in licensed bus/limo services
Stationary vehicle in permitted location

quiz.q: Where must open alcohol be stored when travelling in a vehicle in South Australia?
options: It is always prohibited to carry alcohol
quiz.explanation: Open alcohol accessible to driver or passengers is prohibited. Sealed containers stored in the boot are generally permitted.

laws.title: Recreational Cannabis — Decriminalised — civil expiation notice (NOT full legalisation)
laws.subtitle: Controlled Substances Act 1984 (SA) / Summary Offences Act 1953 (SA) — Decriminalised — Expiation Notice (civil fine) for possession up to 100g
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: South Australia has a unique cannabis decriminalisation scheme since 1987. Possession of up to 100g of cannabis or 20g of cannabis resin results in an Expiation Notice (fine) rather than criminal prosecution. Possession of plants up to 1 (non-hydro) is also expiated. However, supply and commercial cultivation remain criminal offences. Cannabis remains prohibited under Commonwealth law (Criminal Code Act 1995) but state enforcement varies.
laws.penalty: Possession ≤100g or ≤1 non-hydro plant: expiation notice (fine ~$300). Failure to pay: court summons and possible criminal record. Supply/trafficking: up to life imprisonment.
exceptions: Medical cannabis with TGA authorisation
ACT adults (personal use/cultivation only in ACT)
Hemp food products (federally permitted)

quiz.q: What is the legal status of recreational cannabis in South Australia?
options: Decriminalised — civil fine only for small amounts
quiz.explanation: South Australia has had a unique cannabis decriminalisation scheme since 1987 — possession of up to 100g is an expiation (civil fine), not a criminal offence. SA is the only Australian state with this scheme.

laws.title: Medical Cannabis — TGA Federal Scheme
laws.subtitle: Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 (Cth) — TGA approval required
laws.fullDescription: Medical cannabis in Australia is federally regulated by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA). Patients need a prescription from an authorised prescriber or through the Special Access Scheme (SAS). Since 2016, TGA has approved thousands of practitioners and tens of thousands of patients. South Australia follows the federal scheme.
laws.penalty: Possessing cannabis without valid authorisation: state drug law penalties apply.
exceptions: Authorised prescribers issue scripts directly
SAS-B allows practitioners to prescribe to specific patients
State/territory health departments may have additional rules

quiz.q: Which body regulates access to medical cannabis in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Medical cannabis is federally regulated in Australia by the TGA through the Special Access Scheme and Authorised Prescriber pathways.

laws.title: Firearms — National Firearms Agreement (NFA)
laws.subtitle: Firearms Act (state) + NFA 1996 — Strict licensing required
laws.fullDescription: Australia overhauled its firearm laws following the 1996 Port Arthur massacre. The National Firearms Agreement banned semi-automatic and pump-action rifles and shotguns. South Australia: NSW has a firearms registry and strict Category A–H licensing system. Semi-automatics and pump-action shotguns (Categories C/D) banned except for farmers/occupational. All firearms require a licence and registration. A 28-day waiting period and genuine reason (sport/hunting/occupation) required.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed possession of a firearm: up to 14 years imprisonment (varies by state and firearm category).
exceptions: Licensed owners with genuine reason
Police and defence forces
Farmers for pest control (with licence)

quiz.q: What major event triggered Australia's strict National Firearms Agreement in 1996?
quiz.explanation: The Port Arthur massacre (35 killed, 23 wounded) in 1996 led Prime Minister Howard to introduce the NFA, which banned most semi-automatic weapons and led to a national buyback of 650,000+ firearms.

laws.title: Firearms Licence — Background Check & Safe Storage
laws.subtitle: Firearms Act 1996 (NSW) — Mandatory licence, check & storage
laws.fullDescription: All firearms owners in South Australia must hold a valid firearms licence for each category of firearm they own. Police conduct background checks covering criminal history, domestic violence, and mental health. All firearms must be stored unloaded in an approved locked safe, separate from ammunition.
laws.penalty: Improper storage: licence suspension/cancellation, seizure of firearms, fines or imprisonment.
exceptions: Firearms clubs and ranges (supervised use)
Dealers must hold separate dealer's licence
Temporary permit for estates and inheritances

quiz.q: How must firearms be stored in Australia?
options: Unloaded in a locked approved safe, ammo separate
In a vehicle for quick access
quiz.explanation: Australian law requires all firearms to be stored unloaded in an approved locked safe with ammunition stored separately — even in the owner's home.

laws.title: Self-Defence — Common Law & Criminal Code
laws.subtitle: Criminal Law Consolidation Act 1935 (SA) s. 15 — Proportionate force; no 'Stand Your Ground'
laws.fullDescription: Self-defence in South Australia is governed by Criminal Law Consolidation Act 1935 (SA) s. 15. A person may use such force as is reasonably necessary to defend themselves or another. There is no 'Stand Your Ground' law in Australia — retreat is not legally required but is a factor courts consider. SA codified self-defence in the Criminal Law Consolidation Act. Proportionate force required; no Stand Your Ground doctrine.
laws.penalty: Excessive force negates the self-defence claim; charged as assault or more serious offence.
exceptions: Defending oneself from imminent unlawful force
Defending another person
Defence of property (with stricter limits)
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Criminal Code / Common Law

quiz.q: Does Australia have a 'Stand Your Ground' law like some US states?
options: No — proportional force is required; retreat not mandatory but considered
quiz.explanation: Australia has no Stand Your Ground doctrine. Self-defence requires proportionate force. Whether retreat was possible is one factor courts consider.

laws.title: Minimum Wage — National Minimum Wage
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) s. 294 — Annual wage review
laws.fullDescription: Australia's National Minimum Wage (NMW) is set annually by the Fair Work Commission. As of July 2024, the NMW is $23.23/hour (or $882.80/week for a full-time worker). South Australia workers are covered by the federal system under the Fair Work Act 2009. The National Minimum Wage applies to all states. Most workers in NSW are covered by awards which often exceed the NMW.
laws.penalty: Underpaying wages: Fair Work Ombudsman investigation, back-pay orders, civil penalties up to $18,780 per contravention (individual).
exceptions: Award rates apply in many industries and may exceed NMW
Enterprise agreements may set higher rates
Some state public servants covered by state employment laws
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Commission / Fair Work Act 2009

quiz.q: Who sets Australia's National Minimum Wage?
options: Fair Work Commission through annual review
quiz.explanation: The Fair Work Commission conducts an annual minimum wage review and sets the National Minimum Wage, which applies across Australia.

laws.title: Unfair Dismissal — Fair Work Act Protections
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) Part 3-2 — Protection from unfair dismissal
laws.fullDescription: Unlike US at-will employment, Australia's Fair Work Act provides strong protection against unfair dismissal. Employees covered by the federal system who have completed the minimum employment period (1 year for small businesses, 6 months for others) may apply to the Fair Work Commission if dismissed harshly, unjustly, or unreasonably. SA private sector workers covered by the federal Fair Work Act. SA has its own Industrial Relations Act for state public servants.
laws.penalty: Unfair dismissal remedy: reinstatement or compensation up to 26 weeks' pay (capped at half the high income threshold).
exceptions: Casual employees may have limited access (min 12 months regular service)
High-income employees above the threshold may have different options
Redundancy with genuine severance generally not unfair dismissal
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Act 2009 / Fair Work Commission

quiz.q: How long does an employee generally need to work before they can claim unfair dismissal in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The minimum employment period before a Fair Work Act unfair dismissal claim is 6 months (or 1 year if the employer has fewer than 15 employees).

laws.title: Union Rights & Industrial Action
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) — Right to organise; protected industrial action
laws.fullDescription: The Fair Work Act protects employees' right to join unions, participate in union activities, and take protected industrial action during enterprise bargaining. South Australia: SA has a union presence in manufacturing, healthcare, and public sectors. SA unions are affiliated with SA Unions (the state peak body). Unions are registered with the Fair Work Commission.
laws.penalty: Unprotected industrial action: injunctions, penalties. Employers cannot dismiss workers for union membership.
exceptions: Protected industrial action during bargaining — legal
Right of entry: union officials may enter workplaces with 24 hours notice
General protections: adverse action for exercising workplace rights is prohibited

quiz.q: Can Australian employees take industrial action (e.g. strike) legally?
options: Yes — 'protected' industrial action during enterprise bargaining is legal
quiz.explanation: Protected industrial action during enterprise bargaining is legal under the Fair Work Act, provided notice and procedural requirements are met.

laws.title: Non-Compete Agreements
laws.subtitle: Common Law (Restraint of Trade) — Restraints must be reasonable
laws.fullDescription: Non-compete clauses in South Australia are governed by Common Law (Restraint of Trade). Courts apply a reasonableness test — the restraint must go no further than necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interests. SA courts apply common law reasonableness to non-competes. Overly broad clauses struck down.
laws.penalty: Overly broad restraints struck down as unenforceable; employer may lose protection entirely.
exceptions: Non-solicitation of clients/employees more readily enforced
Sale-of-business restraints treated more leniently
Courts may 'read down' (reduce scope) rather than void entirely

quiz.q: How do Australian courts treat overly broad non-compete clauses?
options: Void — non-competes are illegal in Australia
Scrutinised for reasonableness; overly broad clauses struck down or read down
Only enforceable if the employee was a senior executive
quiz.explanation: Australian courts apply a reasonableness test to non-competes and may 'read down' (reduce scope) or void clauses that go beyond what's necessary to protect legitimate interests.

laws.title: Paid Leave — Annual & Personal/Carer's Leave
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) NES — Minimum leave entitlements
laws.fullDescription: The National Employment Standards (NES) under the Fair Work Act set minimum paid leave: 4 weeks annual leave per year, 10 days personal/carer's leave (sick leave) per year, and 2 days compassionate leave per occasion. These apply to full-time workers covered by the national system. SA provides NES entitlements. SA long service leave: 13 weeks after 10 years.
laws.penalty: Underpaying leave: FWO back-pay orders, penalties.
exceptions: Part-time workers receive proportionate leave
Casual workers receive 25% casual loading instead
Awards and enterprise agreements may provide more generous leave

quiz.q: How many days of paid personal/sick leave per year do full-time employees get under Australia's National Employment Standards?
quiz.explanation: The NES provides 10 days paid personal/carer's leave (sick leave) per year for full-time employees, accruing progressively.

laws.title: Unemployment Benefits — JobSeeker Payment
laws.subtitle: Social Security Act 1991 (Cth) — Federal JobSeeker
laws.fullDescription: Australia's unemployment support — JobSeeker Payment — is federally administered by Services Australia. As of 2024, the base rate is approximately $762.70/fortnight for singles (subject to income and assets tests). SA's manufacturing and services economy means JobSeeker usage is significant, particularly in regional and northern SA. Australia has no province/state-level unemployment insurance system.
laws.penalty: Receiving incorrect payments: repayment required; fraud penalties under the Criminal Code.
exceptions: Mutual obligation requirements (job search activities) must be met
Income and assets tests reduce or eliminate payments for higher earners
Waiting periods may apply depending on circumstances

quiz.q: What is Australia's main unemployment payment called?
quiz.explanation: Australia's unemployment payment is called JobSeeker Payment (formerly Newstart Allowance), administered federally by Services Australia through Centrelink.

laws.title: Workers' Compensation — ReturnToWorkSA
laws.subtitle: Return to Work Act 2014 (SA) — No-fault workplace injury scheme
laws.fullDescription: South Australia's workers' compensation system provides no-fault coverage for workplace injuries and diseases. The scheme is administered by ReturnToWorkSA. ReturnToWorkSA administers SA's workers' compensation scheme, which focuses on early return to work outcomes. In exchange for coverage, injured workers generally cannot sue their employer.
laws.penalty: Employer failure to comply: fines up to $75,000.
exceptions: Self-employed workers not automatically covered
Some contractors may be workers under extended definitions
Comcare covers Commonwealth government employees

quiz.q: What body administers workers' compensation in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: South Australia's workers' compensation is administered by ReturnToWorkSA.

laws.title: Independent Contractors — Classification
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 / Independent Contractors Act 2006 (Cth)
laws.fullDescription: Contractor vs employee classification in Australia is determined by multi-factor analysis (control, equipment, integration). The Fair Work Act 2009 (amended 2022) introduced a new 'employee-like' category and allows workers to challenge sham contracting arrangements. South Australia: SA applies the federal multi-factor contractor test. Sham contracting is unlawful.
laws.penalty: Sham contracting (treating employees as contractors): civil penalties up to $93,900/contravention (company).
exceptions: Genuine business-to-business contractors retain independent status
Written contracts are one factor, not determinative
Digital platform workers ('gig economy') increasingly subject to employee-like protections
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Act 2009 / Independent Contractors Act 2006

quiz.q: What approach does Australia take to determine if someone is an employee or contractor?
options: Multi-factor 'real substance of the relationship' test
quiz.explanation: Australian courts apply a multi-factor test looking at the 'real substance' of the relationship, not just the written contract. Sham contracting is unlawful.

laws.title: Child Labour — Minimum Age & Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 / Fair Work Act (SA) — Children under 15 generally cannot work
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA permits light work from age 15. Children under 15 may work in entertainment with parental consent and appropriate permits. Federal NES restricts child labour in nationally regulated industries. Children must not work during school hours.
laws.penalty: Employing children under minimum age: significant fines.
exceptions: Entertainment industry with parental consent and permit
Family business (limited)
School-based apprenticeships with parental consent

quiz.q: What is the general minimum working age in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: In South Australia, children generally must be at least 15 to work, with restrictions on hours and types of work for those under 18.

laws.title: Pay Equity — Fair Work Act & State Laws
laws.subtitle: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) / Equal Opportunity legislation
laws.fullDescription: Pay equity in Australia is addressed through the Fair Work Commission's work value and minimum wage decisions, and through state/territory anti-discrimination and equal opportunity laws. South Australia: SA participates in federal pay equity reviews. SA Government has equal remuneration commitments. The gender pay gap in Australia is approximately 21.7% (2024, WGEA).
laws.penalty: Pay discrimination: complaints to Fair Work Commission or state equal opportunity body.
exceptions: Work value cases can result in pay rises for female-dominated industries
WGEA (Workplace Gender Equality Agency) reports on employer pay gaps
Enterprise bargaining must not discriminate
laws.sourceLabel: Fair Work Commission / South Australia Equal Opportunity

quiz.q: Which federal agency publishes employer-level gender pay gap data in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Since 2024, WGEA has published employer-level gender pay gap data for organisations with 100+ employees — a world-leading transparency measure.

laws.title: Anti-Discrimination — Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (SA)
laws.subtitle: Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (SA) + federal Acts — Comprehensive protections
laws.fullDescription: South Australia's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (SA) prohibits discrimination in employment, goods/services, and accommodation on grounds including race, sex, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, and more. Federal laws (Racial Discrimination Act, Sex Discrimination Act, Disability Discrimination Act, Age Discrimination Act) also apply. SA's Equal Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination. The Equal Opportunity Commission SA handles complaints.
laws.penalty: Complaints: state tribunal or Australian Human Rights Commission; remedies include compensation, apology, and policy changes.
exceptions: Genuine occupational requirements defence
Special measures (positive discrimination) to promote equality
Religious bodies may have limited exemptions in some states

quiz.q: Which body handles federal anti-discrimination complaints in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) handles federal anti-discrimination complaints; state tribunals handle state-law complaints.

laws.title: Landlord Entry — Notice Required
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 1995 (SA) — 24 hours notice required
laws.fullDescription: South Australia requires landlords to give 24 hours written notice before entering a rental property for non-emergency purposes. SA requires at least 24 hours written notice before landlord entry for routine inspections. Emergency entry allowed without notice.
laws.penalty: Illegal entry: SACAT complaint; compensation.
exceptions: Emergencies (flooding, fire, gas leak)
Tenant consents to immediate entry
Final inspection at end of tenancy with proper notice

quiz.q: How much notice must a landlord give before entering a rental property in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: South Australia requires 24 hours written notice before a landlord can enter a rental property (except for emergencies).

laws.title: Rental Bond — Maximum & Lodgement
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 1995 (SA) — Max bond: 4 weeks' rent (if weekly rent ≤$800); no limit for higher rents; held by Consumer and Business Services (CBS) SA
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA rental bonds are lodged with Consumer and Business Services (CBS) within 14 days. Bonds must be lodged with Consumer and Business Services (CBS) SA (not held by the landlord) and returned within 7 business days of tenancy ending.
laws.penalty: Bond not lodged: SACAT complaint.
exceptions: Bond returned if no claim within required period
Disputes handled by tribunal
Condition report at start prevents disputed claims
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Residential Tenancies / Consumer and Business Services (CBS) SA

quiz.q: Where must rental bonds be lodged in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: In South Australia, rental bonds must be lodged with Consumer and Business Services (CBS) SA — not held by the landlord or agent — to protect tenants.

laws.title: Rent Increases — No rent cap — once per 12 months
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 1995 (SA) — No rent control; increases limited to once per 12 months
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA has no rent cap. Rent increases are limited to once per 12 months with 60 days written notice.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant rent increase: SACAT order.
exceptions: 60 days written notice required
Only one increase permitted per 12-month period

quiz.q: How often can a landlord increase rent in South Australia?
options: No more than once every 12 months
quiz.explanation: SA limits rent increases to once per 12 months with 60 days' notice. No cap on the amount.

laws.title: Eviction — Notice & Tribunal Process
laws.subtitle: Residential Tenancies Act 1995 (SA) — Formal process required; self-help eviction illegal
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA landlords must apply to SACAT for a possession order. SA recently strengthened tenant protections. Landlords cannot change locks, remove belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out — these are illegal 'self-help' evictions.
laws.penalty: Illegal eviction: NCAT compensation order, criminal charge.
exceptions: Tenant can remedy breach before eviction order in many cases
Illegal eviction: tenant entitled to compensation and restoration of possession
Domestic violence provisions allow tenants to end lease safely
laws.sourceLabel: South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT)

quiz.q: What is the correct legal process for a landlord to evict a tenant in Australia?
options: Applying to the state tribunal for a possession order
Calling police to remove the tenant
quiz.explanation: Landlords must obtain a formal possession order from the state tenancy tribunal. Self-help eviction (changing locks, removing possessions) is illegal in all Australian states.

laws.title: Short-Term Rentals (Airbnb/Stayz)
laws.subtitle: Development Act 1993 (SA) / local councils — Regulated by local councils and state planning
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA regulates STR through state planning policies and local council requirements. Adelaide council areas have varying STR rules.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with SEPP: planning penalties.
exceptions: Primary residence (owner-occupied) may have different rules
Strata/body corporate rules may prohibit STR
GST registration required if STR income exceeds $75,000/year

quiz.q: Are short-term rentals regulated in South Australia?
options: Regulated — registration, planning approval, or caps may apply
quiz.explanation: Short-term rentals in South Australia are regulated — local council approval may be required; registration requirements apply in some areas.

laws.title: Land Tax — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Land Tax Act 1936 (SA) — Annual tax on unimproved land value
laws.fullDescription: South Australia levies land tax annually on the total unimproved value of taxable land above a threshold. SA land tax applies to total taxable land value above $534,000 threshold (2024). SA has a progressive land tax rate. Principal place of residence is generally exempt. Land tax is a major revenue source for Australian states.
laws.penalty: Unpaid land tax: penalties, interest, and ultimately a charge on the land.
exceptions: Principal place of residence: exempt in most states
Primary production land: often exempt or concession
Trusts may lose exemptions on primary residence

quiz.q: Is the principal place of residence (family home) subject to land tax in South Australia?
options: No — principal place of residence is generally exempt
Only if the land value exceeds $5M
quiz.explanation: In South Australia, the principal place of residence is generally exempt from land tax. Investment properties and vacant land are taxed.

laws.title: Stamp Duty / Transfer Duty on Property
laws.subtitle: Stamp Duties Act 1923 (SA) — Stamp duty applies
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: South Australia charges stamp duty on property purchases. For a $1M property: approximately $48,830. Stamp duty (called transfer duty in some states) is a major upfront cost of purchasing property in Australia — typically 3–5% of the purchase price.
laws.penalty: Underpaying duty: penalty plus interest.
exceptions: First home buyer concession available for properties under $650,000
Foreign buyers may pay additional surcharges
Commercial property may have different rates

quiz.q: What is stamp duty (transfer duty) in South Australia?
options: A tax paid when purchasing real estate
A federal tax on all investments
quiz.explanation: Stamp duty is a state-based tax paid when purchasing real estate. In South Australia, stamp duty applies — approximately $48,830 on a $1M property.

laws.title: Income Tax — Federal Only (No State Income Tax)
laws.subtitle: Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth) — ATO administers
laws.fullDescription: Australia has no state or territory income taxes. All income tax is federal, administered by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO). Top marginal rate is 45% on income over $180,001 (plus 2% Medicare Levy). South Australia residents are subject to federal income tax like all Australians. NSW residents pay federal income tax only; NSW has no state income tax.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: civil penalties, criminal prosecution, up to 10 years imprisonment for serious fraud.
exceptions: Tax-free threshold: $18,200 (2024-25)
15% concessional rate on superannuation contributions
Capital gains discount: 50% for assets held over 12 months
laws.sourceLabel: Australian Taxation Office / Income Tax Assessment Act 1997

quiz.q: Does any Australian state or territory collect its own income tax?
options: Yes — all states have their own income tax
No — income tax is exclusively federal in Australia
Yes — states collect 10% of federal income tax
quiz.explanation: Unlike Canada or the US, Australia has no state income taxes. All income tax is collected by the federal ATO.

laws.title: GST — Goods and Services Tax (Federal 10%)
laws.subtitle: A New Tax System (Goods and Services Tax) Act 1999 (Cth) — 10% GST
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a federal 10% tax on most goods and services, introduced in July 2000 under the Howard government. GST revenue is distributed to the states and territories. NSW collects no GST directly — revenue distributed from federal pool to states. Most fresh food, health, education, and financial services are GST-free.
laws.penalty: Businesses must register if annual turnover exceeds $75,000 (or $150,000 for non-profits). Non-compliance: ATO audit, penalties.
exceptions: Fresh food (unprocessed) — GST-free
Health and medical services — GST-free
Educational courses — GST-free
Exports — GST-free (input tax credits available)

quiz.q: What is the rate of GST in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Australia's GST rate is 10%, introduced in 2000. Revenue is distributed to states and territories under the federal financial relations framework.

laws.title: Superannuation — Compulsory Retirement Savings
laws.subtitle: Superannuation Guarantee (Administration) Act 1992 (Cth) — 11% SGC
laws.fullDescription: Australia's superannuation system requires employers to contribute a percentage of an employee's earnings to a superannuation fund. The Superannuation Guarantee rate is 11% (2023-24), rising to 12% by 2025. NSW workers are entitled to SG contributions to their chosen super fund. Super is a key feature of Australian employment law and tax policy.
laws.penalty: Underpaying super: ATO SGC liability (rate plus interest plus admin fee), civil penalties, criminal prosecution for deliberate underpayment.
exceptions: Employees over 18 earning more than $450/month (threshold removed 2022 — all earnings now covered)
Self-employed may contribute voluntarily
Super funds must be licenced and regulated by APRA

quiz.q: What is the employer Superannuation Guarantee rate for 2023-24?
quiz.explanation: The Superannuation Guarantee rate is 11% for 2023-24, rising to 11.5% in 2024-25, and 12% from 2025-26.

laws.title: Smoke-Free Legislation — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Tobacco Products Regulation Act 1997 (SA) — Smoking banned in enclosed public spaces
laws.fullDescription: South Australia bans smoking in all enclosed public spaces, workplaces, restaurants, and bars. SA bans smoking in all enclosed public places, outdoor dining, near playgrounds, and at bus/tram stops. Plain packaging of tobacco products has been federal law since 2012 (world-first). The minimum age for purchasing tobacco is 18.
laws.penalty: Individual: $1,250 fine. Occupier allowing smoking: up to $10,000.
exceptions: Outdoor dining areas may be smoke-free under local laws
Designated outdoor smoking areas where provided
Private residences (adults only)

quiz.q: Australia was the first country in the world to introduce which tobacco control measure?
quiz.explanation: Australia introduced mandatory plain (standardised) packaging for tobacco products in 2012 — a world-first. Other countries have since followed.

laws.title: Helmet Law — Mandatory for Cyclists
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic (Miscellaneous) Regulations 2014 (SA) — Helmet compulsory for all cyclists
laws.fullDescription: South Australia requires all cyclists to wear an approved helmet. Australia is unusual globally in mandating helmets for all cyclists of all ages (not just children). SA requires all cyclists to wear an approved helmet.
laws.penalty: No helmet: $188 fine.
exceptions: Helmet exemptions for medical reasons (rare, requires application)
Sikhs may be exempt in some states on religious grounds
E-scooter rules vary by jurisdiction

quiz.q: Is wearing a cycling helmet mandatory for adult cyclists in Australia?
options: No — only children must wear helmets
No — helmets are voluntary for adults
Yes — all cyclists must wear approved helmets
Only on roads, not shared paths
quiz.explanation: All Australian states and territories require all cyclists (including adults) to wear an approved helmet. This is unusual by world standards.

laws.title: Seatbelt Law — Mandatory for All Occupants
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — All occupants must wear seatbelts
laws.fullDescription: South Australia requires all vehicle occupants to wear seatbelts. SA requires all vehicle occupants to wear approved seatbelts. The driver is responsible for ensuring passengers under 16 are correctly restrained. Approved child restraints are compulsory for children based on height/age.
laws.penalty: Not wearing seatbelt: $534 fine + 3 demerit points.
exceptions: Medical exemption with certificate
Vehicles predating seatbelt requirements
Certain heavy vehicles, buses (if not fitted)

quiz.q: Who is responsible for ensuring child passengers are properly restrained in a vehicle in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The driver is legally responsible for ensuring all passengers under 16 are correctly restrained in an approved child restraint or seatbelt.

laws.title: Speed Limits — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — Default: 50 urban / 110 highway
laws.fullDescription: South Australia default speed limits: 50 km/h urban; 110 km/h highways; 25 km/h in some high pedestrian areas; 40 km/h school zones during school hours. Speed cameras (fixed and mobile) are widely used across Australia.
laws.penalty: Speeding: from $168 (up to 10 km/h over) to $1,041 (more than 30 km/h over).
exceptions: School zones: 40 km/h during school hours
Construction zones: reduced limits when workers present
Emergency vehicles exempt when responding

quiz.q: What is the default speed limit in urban/built-up areas in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: The default urban speed limit in South Australia is 50 km/h. Highway limits are typically 110 km/h.

laws.title: Mobile Phone — Any Use Prohibited While Driving
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — Holding a phone in any way while driving is illegal
laws.fullDescription: In South Australia (and across Australia), any use of a handheld mobile phone while driving is illegal — including texting, checking notifications, scrolling, or holding the phone even at traffic lights or in slow-moving traffic. SA has increased mobile phone penalties. Handheld use at any speed is illegal.
laws.penalty: $534 fine + 3 demerit points.
exceptions: Hands-free (mounted, Bluetooth)
Emergency 000 calls
Parked with engine off (not stopped at lights)

quiz.q: Can you briefly check a text at a red light in your car in Australia?
options: Yes — briefly is fine if not driving
No — handheld use is banned even when stopped at lights
quiz.explanation: Handheld mobile phone bans apply even when stopped at traffic lights in all Australian states and territories.

laws.title: Random Breath Testing (RBT) — Mandatory Compliance
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — Police may stop any driver for RBT
laws.fullDescription: Random Breath Testing is legal and widely practised in South Australia. Police can stop any vehicle at any time to conduct a breath test — no reasonable suspicion required. SA Police conduct RBT statewide. Drug testing also conducted on South Australian roads. Australia pioneered RBT; Victoria introduced it in 1976.
laws.penalty: Refusal to submit to RBT: same or greater penalty as drink driving.
exceptions: Must stop when directed by police
Cannot refuse a breath test
Second test on a machine at the station if positive on roadside

quiz.q: Can Australian police conduct a Random Breath Test (RBT) without suspecting the driver of drink driving?
options: Yes — any driver can be stopped at any time for RBT
quiz.explanation: RBT is a cornerstone of Australian road safety. Police can stop any vehicle at any time and require a breath test — no suspicion needed. Refusal is an offence.

laws.title: Keep Left / Move Over — Emergency Vehicles
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — Slow down and move over for emergency vehicles
laws.fullDescription: South Australia requires drivers to move left and slow to 40 km/h (or less) when passing police, ambulance, fire, or breakdown vehicles with lights/sirens activated. SA drivers must slow to 40 km/h and move over for stationary emergency vehicles with lights activated.
laws.penalty: Failure to comply: $534 fine + 3 demerit points.
exceptions: Applies to all emergency and breakdown vehicles with lights activated
If safe lane change not possible, slow to well below speed limit

quiz.q: What speed must drivers slow to when passing a stationary emergency vehicle with lights on in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The 'slow down, move over' rule in Australia requires drivers to slow to 40 km/h when passing stationary emergency or breakdown vehicles with lights activated.

laws.title: Speeding Penalties — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act 1961 (SA) — Graduated fines and demerit points
laws.fullDescription: South Australia uses a graduated speeding penalty system. 30+ km/h over: $1,041 + 5 demerit points + possible suspension. Excessive speed (typically 30+ km/h over limit) results in immediate licence suspension. Demerit points accumulate against your licence.
laws.penalty: 30+ km/h: $1,041 + 5 demerit points. Exceeding limit in speed camera zone: automatic fine.
exceptions: School zone and construction zone penalties typically doubled
Learner/P-plate drivers face lower demerit point thresholds
Demerit point scheme — accumulating points leads to suspension

quiz.q: What typically happens in South Australia if a driver is caught travelling more than 30 km/h over the speed limit?
options: Immediate licence suspension plus a substantial fine
quiz.explanation: In South Australia, driving 30+ km/h over the speed limit typically results in immediate licence suspension and a large fine. The exact threshold varies by state.

laws.title: Age of Majority — 18 in South Australia
laws.subtitle: Age of Majority (Reduction) Act 1971 (SA) — Age of majority is 18
laws.fullDescription: The age of majority in South Australia (and all Australian states/territories) is 18. At 18, individuals gain full legal capacity — they can vote, enter binding contracts, consume alcohol, and are tried as adults in criminal proceedings. NSW follows the national standard of 18 as the age of majority.
laws.penalty: Minors' contracts are generally voidable at their option.
exceptions: Children may have some legal standing earlier (e.g., 16 for employment contracts)
Gillick competence allows younger minors to make some medical decisions
Age of criminal responsibility is 10 federally (proposed reform to raise)
laws.sourceLabel: Age of Majority Act / South Australia

quiz.q: What is the age of majority in all Australian states and territories?
quiz.explanation: The age of majority is 18 across all Australian states and territories — the age at which full legal rights and responsibilities attach.

laws.title: Voting — Compulsory in Australia
laws.subtitle: Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918 (Cth) — Voting is compulsory
laws.fullDescription: Australia has compulsory voting for all citizens aged 18+ in federal elections (since 1924) and South Australia also has compulsory voting in state elections, administered by the Electoral Commission of South Australia. Failure to vote without a valid reason results in a fine. Australia is one of fewer than 25 countries globally with compulsory voting.
laws.penalty: Failure to vote without valid reason: $20 administrative penalty (federal), rising to court fine if not paid.
exceptions: Valid excuses: illness, remote location, religious objection (with evidence)
Overseas Australians on the electoral roll must enrol
Informal (blank/spoiled) voting is legally permitted
laws.sourceLabel: Australian Electoral Commission / State Electoral Commission

quiz.q: Is voting compulsory for eligible Australian citizens?
options: Yes — voting is compulsory for citizens 18+
Only for federal elections, not state
Only if you are enrolled to vote
quiz.explanation: Voting is compulsory for all enrolled Australian citizens 18+. Australia has had compulsory voting since 1924 — one of the few countries in the world to mandate it.

laws.title: Jury Duty — Compulsory for Eligible Citizens
laws.subtitle: Juries Act 1927 (SA) — Random selection from electoral roll
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA jurors drawn from electoral roll. 12-person juries for serious criminal trials. Jurors are selected randomly from the electoral roll. Serving on a jury is a legal obligation for eligible citizens.
laws.penalty: Failure to attend without excuse: fines or contempt of court.
exceptions: Certain professions may be excluded (judges, lawyers, police, medical professionals in some states)
Genuine hardship may justify excuse or deferral
Non-citizens not on the electoral roll are not eligible

quiz.q: How are jurors selected in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Jurors in Australia are selected randomly from the electoral roll — the register of enrolled voters.

laws.title: Mandatory Reporting — Child Abuse & Neglect
laws.subtitle: Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 (SA) s. 30 — Mandatory reporters must report
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA mandates specific professional groups to report reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect to the Department for Child Protection. Mandatory reporters are required to report to child protection authorities (not police) when they form a reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect.
laws.penalty: Failure to report: up to $10,000 fine.
exceptions: Good faith reports protected from civil/criminal liability
Report may be made anonymously
Does not require certainty — reasonable belief/suspicion is sufficient

quiz.q: Who is generally required to make mandatory reports of child abuse in Australian states?
options: Specified professionals (teachers, doctors, social workers, etc.) — varies by state
quiz.explanation: Most Australian states mandate specific professionals (teachers, doctors, nurses, social workers, etc.) to report suspected child abuse. Some states (e.g., NSW) extend this to all adults.

laws.title: Age of Consent — 17 in South Australia
laws.subtitle: Criminal Law Consolidation Act 1935 (SA) — Age of consent: 17
laws.fullDescription: The age of consent in South Australia is 17. South Australia's age of consent is 17 — the highest of any Australian state or territory (most states have 16). Sexual activity with persons under 17 is a serious criminal offence in SA. Special rules apply where there is a relationship of authority/trust (age raised to 18). Child abuse material offences apply regardless of consent.
laws.penalty: Sexual activity with persons under the age of consent: serious criminal offence with substantial imprisonment terms.
exceptions: Close-in-age provisions exist in some states
No exception for positions of trust — age raised to 18
Marriage does not lower the age of consent (minimum marriage age is 18 federally)
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Criminal Code / Crimes Act

quiz.q: What is the age of consent in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: The age of consent in South Australia is 17. Sexual activity with persons under this age is a serious criminal offence.

laws.title: Age of Criminal Responsibility — Doli Incapax
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code (federal proposal: raise to 14) — Currently 10
laws.fullDescription: Australia's age of criminal responsibility is 10 — children aged 10 or older can be charged with criminal offences. Children 10–13 have a rebuttable presumption (doli incapax) that they did not understand their actions were seriously wrong. South Australia: SA has the national minimum age of 10. SA has youth diversion and the Youth Justice Court. A federal review has proposed raising the minimum age to 14, in line with international standards.
laws.penalty: Children in conflict with the law are dealt with in Children's/Youth Courts.
exceptions: Doli incapax presumption (ages 10–13): prosecution must rebut
Children's Courts aim for rehabilitation over punishment
Detention is a last resort for juveniles
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Youth Justice / Crimes Act

quiz.q: What is the current minimum age of criminal responsibility in Australian states?
quiz.explanation: The minimum age of criminal responsibility in Australia is 10 — one of the lowest in the world. Advocacy groups and a federal review have called for it to be raised to 14.

laws.title: Youth Curfew Laws — South Australia
laws.subtitle: No general curfew law — No general youth curfew
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA has no general youth curfew law. Courts impose individual curfew conditions on young offenders. Curfew orders may also be imposed by courts as conditions of bail or supervised release for individual young offenders.
laws.penalty: Curfew breach: police may take minor home; court consequences for ordered curfews.
exceptions: Court-ordered curfews for individual young offenders
Police may return young people home for welfare reasons
Family law curfew conditions may exist in parenting orders

quiz.q: Do Australian states have widespread general youth curfew laws?
options: Yes — all states have 10 PM curfews
Generally no — courts impose individual curfews; few general laws
quiz.explanation: Most Australian states do not have broad general youth curfew laws. Courts impose curfews on individual young offenders as conditions of bail/supervision.

laws.title: Corporal Punishment — Schools Banned; Home Restricted
laws.subtitle: Criminal Law Consolidation Act 1935 (SA) — Schools: banned; parents: limited defence
laws.fullDescription: Corporal punishment in all Australian schools (government and private) is banned. South Australia: Corporal punishment banned in all SA schools. Parents retain a limited reasonable chastisement defence but it is narrowly construed. Parents retain a common law 'lawful correction' defence for physical discipline that is reasonable and moderate — but this is being progressively restricted.
laws.penalty: Excessive physical punishment of children: assault charges.
exceptions: 'Lawful correction' defence for parents only — schools have no defence
Must be reasonable and moderate — no implements, not to head/face
ACT has prohibited all corporal punishment including by parents
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Education Act / Criminal Code

quiz.q: Is corporal punishment (physical discipline) permitted in Australian schools?
options: No — banned in all schools (government and private)
quiz.explanation: Corporal punishment is banned in all Australian schools. Parents retain a limited 'lawful correction' defence for home discipline, though this varies by state.

laws.title: Home Schooling — Regulated in South Australia
laws.subtitle: Education and Early Childhood Services (Registration and Standards) Act 2011 (SA) — Registration required
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: Home education is legal in SA. Parents must register with the Department for Education. All children of compulsory school age must be enrolled in a registered school or approved home education program.
laws.penalty: Failure to register while home educating: fine.
exceptions: Parents need not be qualified teachers in most states
Curriculum requirements vary by state
Regular assessments or reporting may be required

quiz.q: Is home education legal in South Australia?
options: Illegal — all children must attend school
Legal but requires registration and compliance with curriculum requirements
quiz.explanation: Home education is legal in South Australia but requires registration with the Department for Education and curriculum compliance.

laws.title: 'No Jab, No Pay' & 'No Jab, No Play'
laws.subtitle: Family Assistance Legislation Amendment Act 2015 + state laws
laws.fullDescription: Australia's 'No Jab, No Pay' federal policy (2016) ties family payments to children's vaccination status — unvaccinated children of parents who refuse vaccination lose access to childcare benefit/rebate and Family Tax Benefit supplements. South Australia: SA enforces No Jab No Play for childcare and preschool services. Medical exemptions apply. The 'No Jab, No Play' policy in many states limits unvaccinated children's access to childcare.
laws.penalty: Loss of federal childcare benefit and Family Tax Benefit supplements for non-compliant families.
exceptions: Medical exemptions available
Religious/conscientious exemptions removed from federal law in 2016
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and children in remote areas have separate pathways

quiz.q: What is Australia's 'No Jab, No Pay' policy?
options: A police fine for not vaccinating
A policy requiring vaccination to enter Australia
Federal family payments tied to children's vaccination status
quiz.explanation: 'No Jab, No Pay' links federal family payments to vaccination compliance. Conscientious objection exemptions were removed in 2016 — only medical exemptions remain.

laws.title: Abortion — Legal in South Australia
laws.subtitle: Termination of Pregnancy Act 2021 (SA) — Decriminalised and regulated
laws.fullDescription: Abortion has been decriminalised across all Australian states and territories. South Australia: South Australia was the LAST Australian state to decriminalise abortion, passing the Termination of Pregnancy Act in 2021. Previously, abortion was regulated under the 1969 Criminal Law Consolidation Act. Now legal to 22 weeks and 6 days on request; after that with clinical and committee assessment. Access is governed by state health legislation. Medicare covers abortion under certain conditions.
laws.penalty: Performing an abortion outside lawful provisions: criminal offence in some states (for practitioners).
exceptions: Gestational limits apply (vary by state)
After gestational limit: two doctors' approval or multidisciplinary review
Conscientious objection: practitioners must refer
Safe access zones around clinics in most states
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Termination of Pregnancy Act

quiz.q: Is abortion legal in all Australian states and territories?
options: No — still illegal in some states
Yes — decriminalised and regulated in all states and territories
Only federally — states cannot legalise it
quiz.explanation: Abortion has been fully decriminalised across all Australian states and territories — the last to do so was South Australia in 2021.

laws.title: Death Penalty — Abolished in Australia
laws.subtitle: Death Penalty Abolition Act 1973 (Cth) — Federally abolished
laws.fullDescription: Australia abolished the death penalty federally in 1973 and in all states by 1985. The last execution in Australia was Ronald Ryan in Victoria in 1967. Australia also will not extradite individuals to face the death penalty without assurances. SA abolished capital punishment in 1976. The last execution in SA was in 1964.
laws.penalty: N/A — capital punishment does not exist in Australia.
exceptions: Australia extradites only with death penalty assurances (applies to US cases)
Federal abolition prevents any state from reintroducing it
Life imprisonment is the maximum penalty

quiz.q: When was the death penalty abolished at the federal level in Australia?
quiz.explanation: The Death Penalty Abolition Act 1973 abolished capital punishment for all federal offences. All states followed — Queensland last in 1922, but the last execution was Ronald Ryan in Victoria in 1967.

laws.title: Voluntary Assisted Dying (VAD) — Legal since January 2023
laws.subtitle: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2021 (SA) — Legal for terminally ill adults since January 2023
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: South Australia passed its Voluntary Assisted Dying Act in 2021 (commenced 31 January 2023). Eligible adults with a terminal illness expected to cause death within 12 months may request VAD after two assessments. Victoria was the first Australian state to legalise VAD (2019), followed by all other states and territories by 2024.
laws.penalty: Administering assisted dying outside lawful provisions: serious criminal offence.
exceptions: Must be an Australian resident aged 18+ with a terminal illness
Decision must be voluntary, competent, and enduring (not temporary mental state)
Requires assessment by two doctors; 10-day reflection period
Conscientious objection by practitioners permitted
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Voluntary Assisted Dying Act

quiz.q: Is Voluntary Assisted Dying (VAD) legal in South Australia?
options: Yes — legal for terminally ill adults meeting eligibility criteria
Only in hospitals, not at home
quiz.explanation: SA legalised VAD from January 2023. Notably, SA was also the last state to decriminalise abortion (2021), demonstrating significant recent progressive legal reform.

laws.title: Drug Offences — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Controlled Substances Act 1984 (SA) — State and federal criminal law
laws.fullDescription: Drug offences in South Australia are governed by both state legislation and the Commonwealth Criminal Code. SA has a unique expiation notice scheme for minor cannabis possession. Drug court and diversion programs also available for other substances. Possession of small amounts for personal use may be treated differently from trafficking.
laws.penalty: Cannabis ≤100g: expiation notice (~$300). Supply: up to life imprisonment. Other drugs: varies by category.
exceptions: Drug diversion programs (cautions) for minor possession in most states
Medicinal cannabis is legal with TGA authorisation
Court-ordered treatment as alternative to imprisonment for addicted offenders
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Drug Misuse Act / Criminal Code

quiz.q: How does South Australia typically treat first-time offenders caught with a small amount of cannabis for personal use?
options: May be diverted to a caution or education program
quiz.explanation: Most Australian states have drug diversion programs for minor possession — offering cautions, education, or treatment rather than criminal conviction for first-time offenders.

laws.title: Proceeds of Crime — Confiscation
laws.subtitle: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (Cth) + Criminal Assets Confiscation Act 2005 (SA)
laws.fullDescription: Australia has comprehensive proceeds of crime legislation at both federal and state levels. South Australia: SA allows restraint and forfeiture of assets linked to criminal activity. Civil forfeiture available for serious offences. Assets can be restrained (frozen) before conviction and forfeited after. Civil forfeiture (without criminal conviction) is available in some states.
laws.penalty: Dealing with proceeds of crime: money laundering offence (up to 25 years imprisonment).
exceptions: Innocent owner defence available
Living expenses may be released from restrained funds
Third parties with legitimate interest may claim

quiz.q: Can Australian authorities seize assets before a criminal conviction?
options: No — only after a civil court order
Yes — assets can be restrained before conviction in most states
Only the federal government can seize assets
quiz.explanation: Australian proceeds of crime legislation allows assets to be restrained (frozen) before conviction. Post-conviction forfeiture and (in some states) civil forfeiture without conviction are also available.

laws.title: Spent Convictions — Rehabilitation of Offenders
laws.subtitle: Spent Convictions Act 2009 (SA) — Spent convictions after waiting period
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA convictions become spent after 5 years (summary) or 10 years (indictable) crime-free. Expiation notices do not create criminal records. After a 'crime-free' period, qualifying convictions become 'spent' and need not be disclosed in most circumstances. Serious offences (violence, sexual offences) are not eligible.
laws.penalty: Unlawfully disclosing spent conviction: civil liability.
exceptions: Convictions involving imprisonment over a threshold not eligible
Certain positions (childcare, police, courts) require full disclosure regardless
Federal convictions follow the Crimes Act 1914 spent convictions scheme
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Spent Convictions / Rehabilitation Act

quiz.q: What happens to a 'spent conviction' in Australia?
options: It is erased from all records completely
It need not be disclosed in most circumstances after a crime-free waiting period
It can only be accessed by police
quiz.explanation: A spent conviction need not generally be disclosed after the waiting period. The conviction is not erased but is effectively 'sealed' for most purposes.

laws.title: Solitary Confinement / Segregation in Prisons
laws.subtitle: Correctional Services Act 1982 (SA) — Segregation permitted with oversight
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA has segregation provisions under the Correctional Services Act. The Independent Prisoner Advisory Committee and SA Ombudsman provide oversight. The UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Nelson Mandela Rules) limit solitary confinement to 15 consecutive days as a maximum.
laws.penalty: Extended segregation challenged on human rights grounds; prison authorities face oversight complaints.
exceptions: Segregation for safety (protective custody) vs. punishment
Independent oversight by Ombudsman or Inspector of Custodial Services
Mental health impacts of extended isolation well documented

quiz.q: What international standard limits solitary confinement to a maximum of 15 consecutive days?
options: UN Nelson Mandela Rules (Standard Minimum Rules)
quiz.explanation: The UN Nelson Mandela Rules (2015) define prolonged solitary confinement as more than 15 consecutive days and classify it as cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment.

laws.title: Private Prisons — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Correctional Services Act 1982 (SA) — Has private prisons
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA operates the Mount Gambier Prison under a private contract (MTC/Serco). The Port Augusta, Yatala, and Adelaide Remand Centre are government operated. Australia has a significant private prison sector compared to many comparable nations.
laws.penalty: Private prisons must meet contractual standards; non-compliance results in financial penalties.
exceptions: Private operators (Serco, MTC, Sodexo) operate under government contracts
Government retains oversight through Inspector of Custodial Services
Prisoners retain same legal rights regardless of operator

quiz.q: Does {st} have privately operated prisons?
options: No — all prisons are government operated
Yes — some prisons are operated by private companies under government contract
quiz.explanation: SA has some privately operated correctional facilities alongside government-run prisons.

laws.title: Police Body-Worn Cameras — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Deployed — SA Police body-worn cameras
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: South Australia Police have deployed body-worn cameras across the force. Footage is used in prosecutions and disciplinary investigations. Unlike some jurisdictions, Australia has state/territory specific policies rather than a national mandate.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with BWC policies: disciplinary action; footage is admissible as evidence.
exceptions: Privacy legislation governs footage use and retention
CCTV in prisons/watch-houses separate to BWC
Recordings may be used in prosecutions and disciplinary matters

quiz.q: Does South Australia Police use body-worn cameras?
options: Yes — deployed across the force (or being rolled out)
quiz.explanation: SA Police deployed BWCs across the force — footage used in prosecutions and professional standards.

laws.title: Police Use of Force — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Police Act 1998 (SA) — Proportionate force required
laws.fullDescription: South Australia police use-of-force is governed by Police Act 1998 (SA) and policy frameworks. Force must be necessary and proportionate. SA Police use-of-force governed by the Police Act. The Office for Public Integrity (OPI) and Police Ombudsman provide oversight. Independent oversight is provided by Office for Public Integrity (OPI) SA.
laws.penalty: Excessive force: criminal prosecution, civil liability, disciplinary action.
exceptions: Less-lethal options (Taser, OC spray, batons) preferred where safe
Lethal force only where imminent threat to life
Complaints to police oversight body
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Police Act / Office for Public Integrity (OPI) SA

quiz.q: Which body provides independent oversight of police conduct in South Australia?
quiz.explanation: Office for Public Integrity (OPI) SA independently investigates and oversees police conduct in South Australia.

laws.title: Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Intervention Orders (Prevention of Abuse) Act 2009 (SA) — Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA operates a domestic violence disclosure scheme allowing individuals to ask SAPOL about a partner's history of domestic violence. Disclosure schemes allow people to ask police about a current or former partner's history of domestic violence.
laws.penalty: N/A — disclosure only.
exceptions: Information only disclosed where genuine risk of harm
Recipients advised on safety planning
Proactive disclosure also possible where police identify risk

quiz.q: Does South Australia have a scheme allowing people to ask police about a partner's history of domestic violence?
options: No — police cannot disclose this information
Yes — a formal domestic violence disclosure scheme
Only victims can access this information
quiz.explanation: SA's DV disclosure scheme allows individuals to request information from SAPOL about a current or former partner's history of domestic violence.

laws.title: Racial Vilification & Hate Speech Laws
laws.subtitle: Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) s. 18C + Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (SA)
laws.fullDescription: Federal s. 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act makes it unlawful to do an act likely to 'offend, insult, humiliate, or intimidate' based on race. South Australia: SA has racial vilification provisions under the Equal Opportunity Act. The Equal Opportunity Commission handles civil complaints. Criminal vilification laws apply in some states for incitement to serious racial hatred.
laws.penalty: Civil: EOC complaint. Serious incitement: criminal charges possible.
exceptions: S. 18D exempts artistic, academic, and fair comment in good faith
Criminal vilification requires incitement to hatred, not mere offence
Religious vilification laws also exist in some states (VIC, QLD, TAS, ACT)

quiz.q: What does s. 18C of Australia's Racial Discrimination Act prohibit?
options: Acts that offend, insult, humiliate, or intimidate people based on race
Only government actions based on race
quiz.explanation: Section 18C makes it unlawful (civil) to do an act reasonably likely to 'offend, insult, humiliate, or intimidate' a person because of their race or ethnicity.

laws.title: Family Violence — Protection Orders & Criminal Offences
laws.subtitle: Intervention Orders (Prevention of Abuse) Act 2009 (SA) — DVOs, emergency orders, criminal offences
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA issues Intervention Orders (IOs) for domestic violence protection. SA Police have power to issue Police Orders immediately. Domestic/family violence is a national crisis — Australia's National Plan to End Violence Against Women and Children (2022–2032) sets out a coordinated response.
laws.penalty: IO breach: up to 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Domestic Violence Orders (DVOs) / Apprehended Domestic Violence Orders (ADVOs) available
Emergency protection orders available 24/7
Victim does not have to decide whether to prosecute — police/Crown may proceed independently

quiz.q: Can domestic violence charges proceed without the victim's cooperation in Australia?
options: No — victim must testify and cooperate
No — victim can withdraw charges at any time
Yes — prosecutors may proceed in the public interest with or without victim cooperation
Only if the victim is a child
quiz.explanation: Australian prosecutors can and often do proceed with domestic violence charges independent of the victim's cooperation — recognising that victims may be pressured or fear reprisal.

laws.title: Stalking / Cyberstalking — Criminal Offence
laws.subtitle: Criminal Law Consolidation Act 1935 (SA) s. 19AA — Stalking offences with significant penalties
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA's stalking offence covers persistent conduct causing fear. Cyberstalking explicitly included. Cyberstalking (online harassment, surveillance) is also a serious offence. Protection orders are available through both civil and criminal processes.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Restraining orders/protection orders available
Apprehended violence orders (AVOs) in NSW provide civil protection
Online/cyber harassment now explicitly covered in most state laws

quiz.q: Is cyberstalking (online harassment and surveillance) a criminal offence in Australia?
options: No — only physical stalking is criminal
Yes — covered under stalking/harassment laws in all states
Only if it involves explicit threats
quiz.explanation: Cyberstalking and online harassment are criminal offences across all Australian states and territories, recognising the serious harm caused by digital-based stalking.

laws.title: Privacy — Privacy Act 1988 (Federal)
laws.subtitle: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) — Australian Privacy Principles (APPs)
laws.fullDescription: The federal Privacy Act 1988 governs how organisations handle personal information through 13 Australian Privacy Principles (APPs). The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) oversees compliance. South Australia: SA covered by federal Privacy Act 1988. SA government agencies also subject to the Information Privacy Principles. The Privacy Act is currently under reform to strengthen protections.
laws.penalty: Serious/repeated privacy breaches: up to $50 million penalty (organisations) under 2023 reforms.
exceptions: Small businesses (under $3M turnover) generally exempt
Health service providers — all covered regardless of size
Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) scheme: breaches likely to cause serious harm must be reported
laws.sourceLabel: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)

quiz.q: Which body enforces the Australian Privacy Principles?
options: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
quiz.explanation: The OAIC oversees compliance with the Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles, investigating complaints and taking regulatory action.

laws.title: Online Safety — eSafety Commissioner
laws.subtitle: Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth) — eSafety Commissioner
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Online Safety Act 2021 established the eSafety Commissioner with powers to order removal of online content including cyberbullying material targeting children, non-consensual intimate images, and seriously harmful online content. South Australia residents benefit from this federal framework. SA residents can contact the federal eSafety Commissioner for cyberbullying and NCII removal.
laws.penalty: Platform non-compliance with eSafety notices: fines up to $550,000/day.
exceptions: eSafety can order removal of NCII (non-consensual intimate images) within 24 hours
Basic Online Safety Expectations require platforms to tackle harmful content
Age verification for online pornography under consultation

quiz.q: What power does Australia's eSafety Commissioner have?
options: Issue removal notices to platforms for harmful content
quiz.explanation: The eSafety Commissioner can issue notices requiring social media platforms to remove harmful content — including cyberbullying, NCII, and seriously harmful material. Non-compliance attracts significant fines.

laws.title: Environmental Protection — EPBC Act
laws.subtitle: Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Cth) + state laws
laws.fullDescription: Australia's EPBC Act protects matters of national environmental significance — threatened species, World Heritage areas, Ramsar wetlands, and more. South Australia: SA's Environment Protection Authority (EPA) regulates environment. SA has strong marine park network and biodiversity legislation. State environmental agencies regulate local pollution, land clearing, and development.
laws.penalty: EPBC breaches: civil penalties up to $22.5M for companies; criminal prosecution for serious offences.
exceptions: Referral required for significant impacts on EPBC matters
Indigenous protected areas recognised
Climate change listed as a key threatening process under review
laws.sourceLabel: EPBC Act / South Australia Environment Protection

quiz.q: What does Australia's EPBC Act protect?
options: Matters of national environmental significance (threatened species, World Heritage, Ramsar wetlands, etc.)
quiz.explanation: The EPBC Act protects matters of national environmental significance, including threatened species and communities, World Heritage areas, Ramsar wetlands, and migratory species.

laws.title: Renewable Energy — South Australia's Grid
laws.subtitle: South Australian Electricity Supply Industry Act (SA) — ~70%+ renewables — world-leading
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: South Australia is a world leader in renewable energy. SA generates more than 70% of electricity from wind and solar — among the highest renewable penetrations of any grid globally. SA has led on battery storage (Tesla big battery at Hornsdale). Australia's federal Renewable Energy Target (RET) has driven significant investment in wind and solar. Australia ranks among the world's fastest-growing solar markets per capita.
laws.penalty: N/A — renewable energy targets are policy/regulatory.
exceptions: Rooftop solar very popular — Australia has highest per-capita uptake globally
Feed-in tariffs vary by state
Large-scale renewables expanding rapidly

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of South Australia's electricity comes from renewable sources?
quiz.explanation: As of 2024, approximately ~70% of South Australia's electricity comes from renewable sources. Renewables are rapidly expanding across all states.

laws.title: Single-Use Plastics — Bans Across Australia
laws.subtitle: Environment Protection (Plastic Products) Policy 2021 (SA) — Comprehensive bans in effect
laws.fullDescription: All Australian states and territories have banned lightweight single-use plastic bags. South Australia: SA was the FIRST Australian state to ban lightweight plastic bags (2009) and has since extended bans to straws, cutlery, polystyrene, and other single-use plastics. Additional bans on straws, cutlery, and food containers are being rolled out.
laws.penalty: Supply of banned items: fines up to $20,000 (individual).
exceptions: Reusable bags, paper bags, and heavy-duty bags permitted
Medical/healthcare plastic items exempt
Dry cleaning bags and some specialty bags may be exempt

quiz.q: Are single-use lightweight plastic bags banned in Australia?
options: Yes — banned in all states and territories
Only in supermarkets, not in general retail
quiz.explanation: All Australian states and territories have banned lightweight single-use plastic bags. The bans have been progressively extended to other single-use plastics.

laws.title: Container Deposit Scheme (CDS) — South Australia
laws.subtitle: Environment Protection Act 1993 (SA) — Container Deposit Legislation — Australia's FIRST CDS — since 1977
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: South Australia pioneered container deposits in Australia — the SA container deposit scheme has operated since 1977 (originally 5¢, now 10¢). SA was the inspiration for all other Australian CDS programs. The 10¢ deposit incentivises return and recycling of eligible beverage containers.
laws.penalty: Operating an unauthorised return point: fine.
exceptions: Not all containers eligible — alcohol over certain sizes may differ
Network of return points and reverse vending machines
Charities often benefit from donated refund points

quiz.q: What is the refund amount per eligible container returned under South Australia's Container Deposit Scheme?
quiz.explanation: South Australia's CDS provides a 10 cent refund per eligible container returned — incentivising recycling and reducing litter.

laws.title: Animal Cruelty — Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act
laws.subtitle: Animal Welfare Act 1985 (SA) — Cruelty and neglect prohibited
laws.fullDescription: South Australia's SA's Animal Welfare Act prohibits cruelty. RSPCA SA and Primary Industries and Regions SA (PIRSA) enforce. RSPCA and inspectors have enforcement powers. Penalties have increased significantly in recent years.
laws.penalty: Up to $100,000 (corporation) or 4 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Farming practices under approved codes of practice may be exempt
Veterinary procedures
Pest animal control under approved methods
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia RSPCA / Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act

quiz.q: Which organisation primarily enforces animal cruelty laws in Australian states?
quiz.explanation: The RSPCA (Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) is the primary enforcement body for animal cruelty legislation in Australian states and territories.

laws.title: Exotic & Dangerous Animals as Pets
laws.subtitle: National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972 (SA) / Biosecurity Act 2017 — Strict regulation; many species prohibited
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA prohibits keeping most wildlife without permits. Unique SA fauna (hairy-nosed wombat, leafy sea dragon) strictly protected. The importation of most exotic animals is strictly controlled under federal law (EPBC Act, Customs Act). Native wildlife cannot be kept as pets without a permit in most states.
laws.penalty: Keeping prohibited species: up to $44,000 fine.
exceptions: Licensed wildlife sanctuaries and research facilities
Some native species permitted as pets in specific states (e.g., sugar gliders in some)
Zoos under strict licensing
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Biodiversity Conservation / EPBC Act

quiz.q: Can most exotic animals (e.g., lions, tigers, primates) be kept as pets in Australia?
options: Yes — if bought from a licenced dealer
No — most exotic and many native animals are prohibited without special permits
quiz.explanation: Australia's strict biosecurity laws and wildlife protection legislation prohibit most exotic animals as pets. Even many native species require permits to keep.

laws.title: Fireworks — Strictly Regulated
laws.subtitle: Explosives Act 1936 (SA) — Consumer fireworks heavily restricted
laws.fullDescription: South Australia: SA bans consumer fireworks. Only licensed pyrotechnicians may operate fireworks for approved public displays. Unlike many countries, most Australian states ban consumer fireworks entirely — professional licensed operators only.
laws.penalty: Illegal fireworks: up to $22,000 fine.
exceptions: Professional fireworks operators require licence
Approved public displays only
NT has the most permissive laws — Territory Day (1 July) allows limited personal use
laws.sourceLabel: South Australia Explosives / Dangerous Goods Act

quiz.q: Which Australian territory uniquely allows limited personal fireworks use on Territory Day (1 July)?
quiz.explanation: The Northern Territory uniquely permits limited personal fireworks use on Territory Day (1 July). Other states and the ACT generally ban consumer fireworks — professional displays only.

laws.title: Gambling — State-Regulated
laws.subtitle: Casino Act 1997 / Lottery and Gaming Act (SA) — Regulated by Consumer and Business Services (CBS) SA
laws.fullDescription: Gambling in South Australia is regulated by Consumer and Business Services (CBS) SA. SA has SkyCity Adelaide casino and poker machines in hotels and clubs. SA has introduced mandatory pre-commitment (MyCash) technology on all EGMs. Australia has one of the highest gambling expenditures per capita in the world — driven largely by electronic gaming machines (pokies).
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed gambling: significant criminal penalties.
exceptions: Online gambling regulated by federal Interactive Gambling Act 2001
In-play sports betting online is prohibited (federal)
Problem gambling: mandatory self-exclusion schemes in all states

quiz.q: Australia has one of the world's highest gambling expenditures per capita, driven primarily by what type of gambling device?
quiz.explanation: Australia has one of the world's highest gambling losses per adult, driven largely by electronic gaming machines (pokies). There are approximately 200,000 poker machines across Australia.

laws.title: Online Gambling — Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (Cth)
laws.subtitle: Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (Cth) — In-play betting banned online
laws.fullDescription: The federal Interactive Gambling Act 2001 (IGA) regulates online gambling in Australia. It prohibits Australian-based operators from offering online casino games (pokies, roulette, blackjack) to Australians. In-play (live) sports betting online is also prohibited. SA residents subject to the federal IGA. Online casino games prohibited for Australians. Licensed Australian sports betting websites are permitted for pre-game wagering.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed online gambling provision: up to $1.1M per day (companies).
exceptions: Sports betting licensed in each state — pre-game online permitted
Fantasy sports with prizes may be exempt
VPNs to access foreign gambling sites violate the spirit of the IGA

quiz.q: What does Australia's Interactive Gambling Act prohibit?
options: All online betting including sports wagering
Online casino games and in-play sports betting for Australian users
quiz.explanation: The IGA prohibits online casino-style games (pokies, roulette) and in-play sports betting for Australians, while allowing licensed sports betting platforms for pre-game wagering.

laws.title: Right to Repair — Emerging in Australia
laws.subtitle: Australian Consumer Law (ACL) — ACL guarantees apply; no specific right-to-repair law
